full_text:
The barber stroked his chin and recounted the adventure of his fourth brother, Al-Kuz:

"My fourth brother, Al-Kuz, was a butcher in Baghdad who owned a well-stocked stall in the meat bazaar. He was prosperous and respected, but he possessed a fatal flaw: whenever an opportunity arose to make an extraordinary profit without labor, his common sense vanished like steam.

One morning, an aged stranger with a white beard and piercing eyes approached the stall. He purchased a fat quarter of mutton, paid with crisp, shining gold dinars, and departed without asking for change. For five successive days, the stranger returned, buying meat and paying with the same bright gold coins. Al-Kuz, overjoyed by this wealthy patron, locked the coins in a special cedar chest beneath his counter.

On the sixth day, when the butcher went to open his chest to purchase new sheep from the Bedouin drovers, he unlocked the lid and gasped in horror. The cedar chest contained not a single gold coin, but only dried round leaves cut from the fig tree! The mysterious stranger had been an adept in optical illusions, projecting a temporary glamour over worthless foliage.

Enraged by the fraud, Al-Kuz stood in his stall, shouting curses against all magicians. At that moment, an honest customer stepped up and asked to purchase a cut of beef. Al-Kuz, blinded by fury, mistook the innocent citizen for the sorcerer’s accomplice, seized his meat cleaver, and threatened the crowd. The neighbors summoned the police, who searched the stall and discovered the cedar chest filled with strange leaves.

The superstitious magistrate declared that Al-Kuz was practicing unlawful witchcraft in the meat market! The butcher was sentenced to fifty lashes, his stall was confiscated, and he was banished beyond the city walls. He came to my house penniless and bruised, weeping over his ruined trade, learning too late that easy gold often turns to withered leaves in the hand of the greedy."
moral: Greed and dealing in dubious goods bring sudden ruin upon the merchant who abandons fair trading.
